text:
Global smartphone purchases have collapsed.

Worldwide smartphone shipments dropped -22.0% YoY in Q3 2026, to 255.3 million units, their largest quarterly decline on record.

Samsung's shipments fell -5.8% YoY, to 57.8 million units, while Apple's declined -4.0% to 57.3 million units.

At the same time, Xiaomi shipments fell -29.2% YoY to 30.7 million units, Oppo dropped -34.5%, to 25.6 million units, while Vivo fell -31.5%, to 19.1 million units.

This comes as memory costs have surged +350% since last year, driven by AI-related demand, putting further pressure on smartphone manufacturers.

As a result, soaring component costs are forcing vendors to raise prices and reduce budget-focused offerings, with consumers increasingly keeping their existing devices for longer.

Global smartphone sales are contracting amid surging prices.

text:
When I was writing Unreal Engine 1, my time was divided as follows:

- Around 30% went to seriously deep coding on hard problems: assembly language texture mappers, C++ BSP trees, data persistence, object oriented systems design, and networking.

- Around 70% was just typing and refactoring large bodies of code needed for a complete engine feature set. This was not hard, and while I was doing it my mind was mostly on the deeper coding topics, thinking and planning for what's next. It didn't feel much different from vibe coding today, except that it was just me typing code on an IBM Model M keyboard rather than prompting it and reviewing the results.

So, it has always seemed perfectly logical that we would rely on AI for that 70%, once the AI could do it with a similar quality standard as we could, which has never been perfection. It came as no surprise that, after a few years of AI model evolution, it was able to take the reigns on that 70% and free up programmers' time for more valuable tasks.

text:
There are graveyards full of people who thought they had more time.

These individuals were busy making plans for the future. They had dreams and aspirations, always telling themselves “one day…”

That day never came though. Each person ran out of time.

This realization first struck me while I was watching the 2011 movie starring Justin Timberlake, “In Time.” Here is the premise:

"In 2169, people are genetically engineered to stop aging on their 25th birthday. This is when a one-year countdown on their forearm begins. When the countdown reaches zero, the person “times out” and dies instantly.

Time is a universal currency that can be transferred directly between people or time can be earned by working at a company. The wealthiest people have so much time it is nearly unlimited, while the poorest people in the film are constantly close to running out unless they find a way to acquire more."

We may not have clocks built into our forearms, but there is an invisible clock counting down the moments until we take our last breath.

You won’t know when it is going to happen. Sometimes there are signs like declining health, but other times death appears in an instant without warning. The uncertainty can make people uneasy. But the anxiety won’t change the reality.

I have found the best way to deal with an unknown future is to live vigorously in the current moment. If you want to do something, go do it sooner rather than later. Take that vacation you have been dreaming about. Start

text:
McDonald’s actually does have best-tasting Coke in the world and here a few reasons: 

▫️Coca-Cola ships Coke/Diet Coke syrup to McDonald’s in specially-designed 75 gallon stainless steel containers and pumped directly into store machines.

▫️ Metal preserves taste better than plastic bags, which is how every other customers gets their syrup (Coca-Cola reps are also forbidden from selling syrup at a lower cost than what McDonald’s pays).

▫️Syrup machines frequently tweaked and calibrated to ensure taste is consistently strong since McDonald’s pours drinks with certain amount of ice which dilutes when melts.

▫️McDonald’s has specialized water filtration system at every location (tastes better) and cooling system (drink always consistently same cold temperature and cooler water holds more carbonation aka fizz)

Coca-Cola sends employees to do frequent quality checks at McDonald’s locations.

The McDonald’s and Coca-Cola partnership dates back to 1955 and goes deep. 

McDonald’s is the largest restaurant partner ($1B+ a year) and only company within Coca-Cola that has its own division. When Coca-Cola reps are asked about the largest markets, they often say “US, Japan, Germany and McDonald’s.”

Skyrocketing costs are crushing New York restaurants.

text:
This is the new Tesla Roadster's fan and suction system, which the company filed a patent for in April 2025.

Sides skirts and front and rear skirts deploy under the battery pack, sucking the car down at ~2G. Because the skirts can move, they have some compliance, so they can deal with road bumps, road debris, etc. As the speed of the Roadster increases, the front and rear skirts retract to allow for air-flow (venturi effect) under the vehicle.

Tesla: "Our multi-mode fan and ground sealing system acts as a downforce generator, pulling air out from beneath the vehicle. This provides enough suction to hold the vehicle upside down, even when stationary. Powered fans and active wings maximize traction and cornering speeds in all conditions, achieving massive downforce at zero speed."

In their patent, Tesla said: "In the first mode, a complete set of skirts creates a fully sealed bounded region under the vehicle with central fans generating maximum downforce at low speeds on smooth surfaces. In the second mode, a subset of skirts (primarily side skirts) modifies the bounded region while all fans operate to provide downforce in dynamic driving conditions with uneven surfaces. The system includes a control mechanism to selectively deploy skirts and operate fans based on driving conditions, optimizing between maximum downforce at low speeds and improved performance over varying terrain at higher speeds."

en_summary: @cullenroche: MMTers misread reserve accounting; total Fed remittances matter, not IORB alone, and the Fed's recent operating losses have been net stimulative versus prior years' large remittances.
ko_summary: @cullenroche: MMT론자들은 지준 회계를 잘못 이해한다. 중요한 건 IORB 단독이 아니라 연준의 총 송금이며 최근 연준 손실은 과거 대규모 송금 대비 순부양적이었다.
text:
It’s becoming clear that MMTers have a worse understanding of reserve accounting than we thought. 

What matters is the total remittances, not IORB in isolation. And yes, in recent years the Fed has been operating at a loss, which has been net stimulative relative to the large positive remittances of prior years even though this income effect was offset by the tighter credit conditions that accompanied the rate hikes, which were a clear net drag and help explain why inflation fell after 2022.

What’s even more off-base about the idea that this might cause inflation is that the remittances matter in rate of change, not just levels. Saying “there’s $500B of new income because of IORB” doesn’t mean we got inflation from it. If you got $100B every year for 5 years you don’t get ongoing inflation because the rate of change isn’t changing. And in recent years the net interest impact has been improving as the Fed’s annual losses have shrunk substantially, meaning the incremental addition to the consolidated government deficit from this channel has been getting smaller, not larger. They have the direction of the flow backwards and this exercise explains why their theory of inflation has been so wrong in recent years.
